reasoning: Work outward. (1-x^2)^-1 = 1/(1-x^2); 1 minus that is -x^2/(1-x^2); its reciprocal is (1-x^2)/(-x^2); 1 minus that is 1/x^2. So the bracket equals 1/x^2 and the bracket to the power -1/2 is |x|. log10|x| = 1 gives |x| = 10. Checked each option: x=10 gives bracket 1/100 and log 1; x=100 gives log 2; x=1 and x=0 make the expression undefined (division by zero).
solution: Simplify from the inside: \( \left(1-x^{2}\right)^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{1-x^{2}} \), so \( 1-\dfrac{1}{1-x^{2}}=\dfrac{-x^{2}}{1-x^{2}} \), whose reciprocal is \( \dfrac{1-x^{2}}{-x^{2}} \). Subtracting that from \( 1 \) leaves \( \dfrac{1}{x^{2}} \), and \( \left(\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\right)^{-1/2}=|x| \). The equation becomes \( \log_{10}|x|=1 \), so \( x=10 \).

reasoning: f(x) = 4x^2 - 16x + lambda/4 opens upward, so one root in (1,2) and the other in (2,3) requires f(1)>0, f(2)<0, f(3)>0. f(1) = f(3) = lambda/4 - 12 > 0 gives lambda > 48; f(2) = lambda/4 - 16 < 0 gives lambda < 64, which also forces a positive discriminant (256 - 4*lambda > 0). Integers 49 through 63 is 15 values. A scan over integer lambda reproduces exactly 49..63.
solution: The quadratic \( 4x^{2}-16x+\tfrac{\lambda}{4} \) opens upwards, so having one root in \( (1,2) \) and the other in \( (2,3) \) requires \( f(1)>0 \), \( f(2)<0 \) and \( f(3)>0 \). Here \( f(1)=f(3)=\tfrac{\lambda}{4}-12>0 \) gives \( \lambda>48 \), while \( f(2)=\tfrac{\lambda}{4}-16<0 \) gives \( \lambda<64 \) and also makes the discriminant positive. The integers \( 49 \) to \( 63 \) satisfy both, so \( \lambda \) can take \( 15 \) values.

reasoning: 7 + 4*sqrt3 = (2+sqrt3)^2 and 4 + 2*sqrt3 = (sqrt3+1)^2, so the denominator is (2+sqrt3) - (1+sqrt3) = 1 exactly. Numerator 36+49+64+81+100 = 330. Numeric check gives denominator 1.0 and ratio 330.0.
solution: Note that \( 7+4\sqrt{3}=\left(2+\sqrt{3}\right)^{2} \) and \( 4+2\sqrt{3}=\left(\sqrt{3}+1\right)^{2} \), so the denominator is \( \left(2+\sqrt{3}\right)-\left(1+\sqrt{3}\right)=1 \). The numerator is \( 36+49+64+81+100=330 \). Hence the expression equals \( 330 \).

reasoning: Put S = x+y+z. Then x^2 = y+z = S-x, so x(x+1) = S and 1/(x+1) = x/S; likewise for y and z. The sum is (x+y+z)/S = 1. Sanity check with the solution x=y=z=2: each term is 1/3 and the sum is 1.
solution: Write \( S=x+y+z \). Then \( x^{2}=y+z=S-x \), so \( x(x+1)=S \) and \( \dfrac{1}{x+1}=\dfrac{x}{S} \); the same holds for \( y \) and \( z \). Adding the three terms gives \( \dfrac{x+y+z}{S}=1 \).

reasoning: Units: 9+7+8 = 24, write 4 carry 2 (matches the 4 in 1114). Hundreds: 5+3+2 = 10 plus the carry from the tens must give 11 (the leading 11 of 1114), so the tens carry is 1 and P+R+Q+2 = 11, i.e. P+R+Q = 9. Maximum Q is therefore 9 with P=R=0. A full search over digit triples confirms 55 solutions with maximum Q = 9.
solution: The units column gives \( 9+7+8=24 \), so \( 4 \) is written and \( 2 \) carried, matching the final digit of \( 1114 \). The hundreds column \( 5+3+2=10 \) together with its incoming carry must read \( 11 \), so the tens column carries \( 1 \) and \( P+R+Q+2=11 \), i.e. \( P+R+Q=9 \). Taking \( P=R=0 \) makes \( Q \) as large as possible, so the maximum value is \( 9 \).

solution: Every remainder is one less than its divisor, so \( n+1 \) must be divisible by \( 2,3,4,5 \) and \( 6 \), that is by their least common multiple \( 60 \). Hence \( n=60k-1 \), giving \( 59, 119, \ldots \). Between \( 0 \) and \( 100 \) only \( 59 \) occurs, so exactly one integer belongs to the set.
If the number is \( n \), the mistaken result exceeds the correct one by \( 8n-\dfrac{n}{8}=2016 \). This is \( \dfrac{63n}{8}=2016 \), so \( n=\dfrac{2016\times 8}{63}=256 \).

reasoning: Real roots require a^2 >= 4b. a=1: none. a=2: b=1. a=3: b=1,2. a=4: b=1,2,3,4. Total 1+2+4 = 7. Enumeration over the 16 pairs returns exactly those 7.
solution: Real roots require the discriminant \( a^{2}-4b\ge 0 \). With \( a=1 \) no value of \( b \) works; \( a=2 \) allows only \( b=1 \); \( a=3 \) allows \( b=1,2 \); and \( a=4 \) allows \( b=1,2,3,4 \). That is \( 1+2+4=7 \) pairs.

reasoning: Let s be the smaller and L the larger. L^2 = 18s and s^2 + L^2 = 208 give s^2 + 18s - 208 = 0, so s = 8 (the positive root), L^2 = 144, L = 12. Difference 12-8 = 4. A search over integer pairs returns only (8,12).
solution: Let the smaller number be \( s \) and the larger be \( L \), so \( L^{2}=18s \). Substituting into \( s^{2}+L^{2}=208 \) gives \( s^{2}+18s-208=0 \), whose positive root is \( s=8 \). Then \( L^{2}=144 \), so \( L=12 \) and the difference is \( 4 \).

reasoning: A - B = {8,9,11,12}, four elements. B - A = {14,15}, two elements. The question asks for the counts in that order, so 4 and 2.
solution: Removing from \( A \) the elements it shares with \( B \) leaves \( A-B=\{8,9,11,12\} \), which has \( 4 \) elements. Removing from \( B \) the elements it shares with \( A \) leaves \( B-A=\{14,15\} \), which has \( 2 \). Taken in the order asked, the counts are \( 4 \) and \( 2 \).

reasoning: In n days he saves 465n paise; this is a whole number of rupees when 100 | 465n, i.e. 20 | 93n. Since gcd(93,20) = 1, n must be a multiple of 20, least 20. A direct scan for the least n making 4.65n an integer returns 20.
solution: In \( n \) days he saves \( 465n \) paise, which is an exact number of rupees only when \( 100 \) divides \( 465n \), that is when \( 20 \) divides \( 93n \). Since \( 93 \) and \( 20 \) have no common factor, \( n \) itself must be a multiple of \( 20 \). The least such number of days is \( 20 \).

reasoning: By the time the winner covers 4 km the other has covered 4*(4/5) = 3.2 km, a gain of 0.8 km. Each pass needs a full lap of 0.25 km gained; 0.8/0.25 = 3.2, so the gain reaches 1, 2 and 3 laps but not 4. Three passes.
solution: When the winner has run the full \( 4 \) km the other has run \( 4\times\tfrac{4}{5}=3.2 \) km, so the winner has gained \( 0.8 \) km. One pass occurs each time the gain reaches a further complete lap of \( 0.25 \) km, and \( \dfrac{0.8}{0.25}=3.2 \). The gain therefore passes one, two and three laps but not four, so the winner passes the other three times.

reasoning: A fraction in lowest terms terminates exactly when its denominator has only 2 and 5 as prime factors. 1600 = 2^6 * 5^2, 8 = 2^3, and 35/50 reduces to 7/10 - all terminate. 17/6 has a factor 3, so it is non-terminating and repeating.
solution: A fraction in lowest terms has a terminating decimal exactly when its denominator has no prime factor other than \( 2 \) and \( 5 \). Here \( 1600=2^{6}\cdot 5^{2} \), \( 8=2^{3} \), and \( \dfrac{35}{50} \) reduces to \( \dfrac{7}{10} \), so all three terminate. Only \( \dfrac{17}{6} \) keeps a factor \( 3 \) in its denominator, so it is the one with a non-terminating repeating expansion.

reasoning: For 25x^2 - 15x + 2 the roots satisfy alpha+beta = 3/5 and alpha*beta = 2/25. The new zeros 1/(2 alpha) and 1/(2 beta) have sum (alpha+beta)/(2 alpha beta) = (3/5)/(4/25) = 15/4 and product 1/(4 alpha beta) = 25/8. So x^2 - (15/4)x + 25/8, i.e. 8x^2 - 30x + 25 after clearing denominators.
solution: For \( 25x^{2}-15x+2 \) the zeros satisfy \( \alpha+\beta=\tfrac{3}{5} \) and \( \alpha\beta=\tfrac{2}{25} \). The new zeros \( \dfrac{1}{2\alpha} \) and \( \dfrac{1}{2\beta} \) then have sum \( \dfrac{\alpha+\beta}{2\alpha\beta}=\dfrac{15}{4} \) and product \( \dfrac{1}{4\alpha\beta}=\dfrac{25}{8} \). The polynomial is \( x^{2}-\tfrac{15}{4}x+\tfrac{25}{8} \), which on clearing denominators is \( 8x^{2}-30x+25 \).

reasoning: 101 is prime and does not divide 2, so Fermat's little theorem gives 2^100 = 1 mod 101. Direct modular exponentiation confirms 1.
solution: Since \( 101 \) is prime and does not divide \( 2 \), Fermat's little theorem gives \( 2^{100}\equiv 1 \pmod{101} \). The remainder is therefore \( 1 \).

reasoning: With W workers, women = W/3 and men = 2W/3. Married women = (1/2)(W/3) = W/6. Married men = (3/4)(2W/3) = W/2. Ratio (W/6):(W/2) = 1:3. The clauses about children are not needed.
solution: Let there be \( W \) workers, so the women number \( \dfrac{W}{3} \) and the men \( \dfrac{2W}{3} \). Married women are \( \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{W}{3}=\dfrac{W}{6} \), while married men are \( \dfrac{3}{4}\cdot\dfrac{2W}{3}=\dfrac{W}{2} \). The ratio is \( \dfrac{W}{6}:\dfrac{W}{2}=1:3 \); the information about children is not needed.

reasoning: B's rate is 1/30 per hour; A does 50% more in the same time so A's rate is 1.5/30 = 1/20. In 12 hours B alone completes 12/30 = 2/5, leaving 3/5. Combined rate 1/30 + 1/20 = 1/12, so the remaining work takes (3/5)/(1/12) = 36/5 = 7.2 hours.
solution: Since \( B \) alone needs \( 30 \) hours, \( B \) works at \( \dfrac{1}{30} \) per hour, and \( A \), doing \( 50\% \) more in the same time, works at \( \dfrac{1}{20} \). In \( 12 \) hours \( B \) completes \( \dfrac{12}{30}=\dfrac{2}{5} \), leaving \( \dfrac{3}{5} \). Their combined rate is \( \dfrac{1}{30}+\dfrac{1}{20}=\dfrac{1}{12} \), so the remainder takes \( \dfrac{3}{5}\div\dfrac{1}{12}=7.2 \) hours.

reasoning: New speed 1.2s means new time t/1.2 = 5t/6. The saving t - 5t/6 = t/6 = 20 minutes, so t = 120 minutes.
solution: Raising the speed by \( 20\% \) multiplies it by \( 1.2 \), so the time becomes \( \dfrac{t}{1.2}=\dfrac{5t}{6} \). The saving is \( t-\dfrac{5t}{6}=\dfrac{t}{6} \), and this equals \( 20 \) minutes. Hence \( t=120 \) minutes.

reasoning: With maximum M and pass mark p: xM/100 + a = p (fails by a) and yM/100 - b = p (exceeds by b). Equating gives a + b = (y-x)M/100, so M = 100(a+b)/(y-x).
solution: Let the maximum marks be \( M \) and the pass mark be \( p \). Falling short by \( a \) gives \( \dfrac{xM}{100}+a=p \), and exceeding by \( b \) gives \( \dfrac{yM}{100}-b=p \). Equating the two yields \( a+b=\dfrac{(y-x)M}{100} \), so \( M=\dfrac{100(a+b)}{y-x} \).

reasoning: Sum of roots: p + q = -p. Product: pq = q, so q(p-1) = 0. If q = 0 then p = 0 (and x^2 = 0 has roots 0,0 as required). If p = 1 then q = -2, and x^2 + x - 2 has roots 1 and -2 as required. So p = 0 or 1; both cases are realisable, which rules out the 'p = 1 only' option.
solution: Because \( p \) and \( q \) are the roots, the sum gives \( p+q=-p \) and the product gives \( pq=q \), i.e. \( q(p-1)=0 \). If \( q=0 \) the first relation forces \( p=0 \), and \( x^{2}=0 \) indeed has both roots \( 0 \). If \( p=1 \) then \( q=-2 \), and \( x^{2}+x-2 \) does have roots \( 1 \) and \( -2 \). Both cases occur, so \( p=0 \) or \( 1 \).

reasoning: Rice = 125/2.5 = 50 per kg. 9 kg rice = 450 = 4 kg pulses, so pulses = 112.5 per kg. 14 kg pulses = 1575 = 1.5 kg tea, so tea = 1050 per kg. 2 kg tea = 2100 = 5 kg nuts, so nuts = 420 per kg. 11 kg nuts = 4620.
solution: Rice costs \( \dfrac{125}{2.5}=50 \) per kg, so \( 9 \) kg of rice costs \( 450 \), making pulses \( \dfrac{450}{4}=112.5 \) per kg. Then \( 14 \) kg of pulses costs \( 1575 \), so tea is \( \dfrac{1575}{1.5}=1050 \) per kg, and \( 2 \) kg of tea costs \( 2100 \), so nuts are \( \dfrac{2100}{5}=420 \) per kg. Hence \( 11 \) kg of nuts costs \( 4620 \) rupees.

reasoning: 1729 = 1^3 + 12^3 = 9^3 + 10^3. A sweep of all pairs of positive cubes up to 12^3 returns exactly those two representations.
solution: Two representations exist: \( 1729=1^{3}+12^{3} \) and \( 1729=9^{3}+10^{3} \). Checking every pair of positive cubes up to \( 12^{3} \) turns up no others, so \( 1729 \) is a sum of two positive cubes in exactly two ways.

reasoning: Take cost price 100. Marked price 120; 10% discount gives selling price 108. Gain = 8 on 100, i.e. 8%.
solution: Take the cost price as \( 100 \). Raising it by \( 20\% \) gives a marked price of \( 120 \), and a \( 10\% \) discount makes the selling price \( 120\times 0.9=108 \). The gain is \( 8 \) on a cost of \( 100 \), that is \( 8\% \).

reasoning: Coprimality only forbids a shared factor. Examples: 2 and 3 (both prime), 3 and 4 (one prime, one composite), 4 and 9 (both composite) - each has HCF 1. All three statements are possible.
solution: Having highest common factor \( 1 \) only means the two numbers share no factor, which places no restriction on whether each is prime or composite. The pairs \( 2,3 \) (both prime), \( 3,4 \) (one prime and one composite) and \( 4,9 \) (both composite) all have highest common factor \( 1 \). So all three statements are correct.

reasoning: For each n, 1 + 1/n^2 + 1/(n+1)^2 = (1 + 1/n - 1/(n+1))^2, so each surd is 1 + 1/n - 1/(n+1). Summing n = 1..2007 gives 2007 + (1 - 1/2008) = 2008 - 1/2008. Numeric summation of all 2007 terms gives 2007.9995019920318, matching 2008 - 1/2008 exactly.
solution: For each \( n \), \( 1+\dfrac{1}{n^{2}}+\dfrac{1}{(n+1)^{2}}=\left(1+\dfrac{1}{n}-\dfrac{1}{n+1}\right)^{2} \), so every surd equals \( 1+\dfrac{1}{n}-\dfrac{1}{n+1} \). Adding these for \( n=1 \) to \( 2007 \) leaves \( 2007 \) from the constant parts and a telescoping remainder \( 1-\dfrac{1}{2008} \). The total is \( 2008-\dfrac{1}{2008} \).

reasoning: Downstream speed = 20/2 = 10 km/h; upstream speed = 4/2 = 2 km/h. Speed of current = (10-2)/2 = 4 km/h (and the boat's still-water speed is 6).
solution: The downstream speed is \( \dfrac{20}{2}=10 \) km/hour and the upstream speed is \( \dfrac{4}{2}=2 \) km/hour. The speed of the current is half their difference, \( \dfrac{10-2}{2}=4 \) km/hour.

reasoning: Odd squared is odd, so x^2 + y^2 is even: statement 1 holds. But an odd square is 1 mod 8, so x^2 + y^2 = 2 mod 8, never a multiple of 4 (e.g. 9 + 25 = 34). Statement 2 fails. So 1 only.
solution: Since \( x \) and \( y \) are odd, \( x^{2} \) and \( y^{2} \) are both odd, so their sum is even and the first statement holds. However an odd square leaves remainder \( 1 \) on division by \( 8 \), so \( x^{2}+y^{2}\equiv 2 \pmod{8} \) and can never be a multiple of \( 4 \); for instance \( 3^{2}+5^{2}=34 \). Only the first statement is correct.

Numeric check: at x = -2 the left side is 9.000, and at x = -0.58496 it is 9.000. Note the options with log(3/2) and log(2/3) are not the same quantity as log3/log2.
solution: Since \( 27^{x/(x-1)}=3^{3x/(x-1)} \), the equation reads \( 2^{x+2}=3^{\,2-3x/(x-1)}=3^{-(x+2)/(x-1)} \). Taking logarithms gives \( (x+2)\left(\log 2+\dfrac{\log 3}{x-1}\right)=0 \), so either \( x+2=0 \) or \( x-1=-\dfrac{\log 3}{\log 2} \). The roots are \( -2 \) and \( 1-\dfrac{\log 3}{\log 2} \).

For \( i=1 \) to \( 12 \) these are \( 12, 22, 30, 36, 40, 42, 42, 40, 36, 30, 22, 12 \), and the largest value \( 42 \) occurs twice, at \( i=6 \) and \( i=7 \). The sum is therefore \( 2^{122}\left(1+4+16+64+256\right)=2^{122}\times 341 \), and \( 341=11\times 31 \). Since the power of two contributes no odd factor, the number is divisible by \( 11 \).

solution: The second expression factorises as \( 4p^{2}+4pq-3q^{2}=(2p+3q)(2p-q) \). Using \( 2p+3q=12 \) turns this into \( 12(2p-q)=126 \), so \( 2p-q=\dfrac{21}{2} \). Solving that with \( 2p+3q=12 \) gives \( q=\dfrac{3}{8} \) and \( p=\dfrac{87}{16} \), so \( p+2q=\dfrac{99}{16} \).

reasoning: Digits = floor(log10 N) + 1. log10(3^30) = 30 * 0.4771 = 14.313, so 14 + 1 = 15. The exact integer 3^30 = 205891132094649 does have 15 digits.
solution: The number of digits of a positive integer \( N \) is \( \lfloor\log_{10}N\rfloor+1 \). Here \( \log_{10}3^{30}=30\times 0.4771=14.313 \), so the count is \( 14+1=15 \).

reasoning: Unit digits of powers of 7 cycle 7, 9, 3, 1 with period 4. 139 = 4*34 + 3, so the unit digit is the third term, 3. Direct check: 7^139 mod 10 = 3.
solution: The unit digits of the powers of \( 7 \) repeat in the cycle \( 7, 9, 3, 1 \), of length \( 4 \). Since \( 139=4\times 34+3 \), the exponent sits at the third place of the cycle. The unit digit is \( 3 \).

reasoning: Each fraction cancels: (x^2+ax+a^2)/(x^3-a^3) = 1/(x-a) and (x^2-ax+a^2)/(x^3+a^3) = 1/(x+a). The difference is 2a/(x^2-a^2). With x = -3a/4, x^2 - a^2 = 9a^2/16 - a^2 = -7a^2/16, so the value is 2a * (-16/(7a^2)) = -32/(7a). Symbolic simplification returns -32/(7a).
solution: Using \( x^{3}-a^{3}=(x-a)\left(x^{2}+ax+a^{2}\right) \) and \( x^{3}+a^{3}=(x+a)\left(x^{2}-ax+a^{2}\right) \), the expression collapses to \( \dfrac{1}{x-a}-\dfrac{1}{x+a}=\dfrac{2a}{x^{2}-a^{2}} \). From \( 4x+3a=0 \) we have \( x=-\dfrac{3a}{4} \), so \( x^{2}-a^{2}=\dfrac{9a^{2}}{16}-a^{2}=-\dfrac{7a^{2}}{16} \). The value is therefore \( -\dfrac{32}{7a} \).

reasoning: X withdraws 2/7 of 700 = 200 after 3 months, leaving 500; after 3 more months he returns 3/5 of 200 = 120, giving 620 for the last 6 months. Money-months: 700*3 + 500*3 + 620*6 = 7320. Y: 600*12 = 7200. Total 14520. X's share = 726 * 7320/14520 = 366 exactly.
solution: After three months \( X \) withdraws \( \dfrac{2}{7}\times 700=200 \), leaving \( 500 \); three months later he returns \( \dfrac{3}{5}\times 200=120 \), leaving \( 620 \) for the final six months. His money-months total \( 700\times 3+500\times 3+620\times 6=7320 \), while \( Y \) contributes \( 600\times 12=7200 \). So \( X \) receives \( 726\times\dfrac{7320}{14520}=366 \) rupees.

reasoning: X fills 1/2 per hour, so from 10 to 11 a.m. it fills half the tank. Together the pipes fill 1/2 + 1/6 = 2/3 per hour, so the remaining half needs (1/2)/(2/3) = 3/4 hour = 45 minutes, ending at 11:45 a.m. Printed oddity, solved as printed: option (a) reads '12:45 hours' where the other three are clock times with a.m./p.m., so it could be read as a duration; either reading leaves 11:45 a.m. as the answer.
solution: Pipe \( X \) fills \( \dfrac{1}{2} \) of the tank each hour, so between \( 10 \) and \( 11 \) it fills half of it. Together the two pipes fill \( \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{6}=\dfrac{2}{3} \) per hour, so the remaining half takes \( \dfrac{1}{2}\div\dfrac{2}{3}=\dfrac{3}{4} \) hour. That is \( 45 \) minutes after \( 11 \), so the tank is full at \( 11{:}45 \) a.m.

reasoning: Relative speed 48+42 = 90 km/h = 25 m/s; in 12 s the trains cover 300 m = L + L/2, so L = 200 m. At 48 km/h = 40/3 m/s for 45 s the train covers 600 m = L + platform, so the platform is 400 m.
solution: Moving in opposite directions the relative speed is \( 48+42=90 \) km/hour \( =25 \) m/s, so in \( 12 \) s the trains together cover \( 300 \) m. That is the sum of the lengths, \( L+\dfrac{L}{2}=\dfrac{3L}{2} \), so \( L=200 \) m. Passing the platform at \( 48 \) km/hour \( =\dfrac{40}{3} \) m/s for \( 45 \) s covers \( 600 \) m, so the platform measures \( 600-200=400 \) m.

solution: Over the same distance the time taken is inversely proportional to the speed, so the times are in the ratio \( \dfrac{1}{2}:\dfrac{1}{3}:\dfrac{1}{4} \). Multiplying every part by \( 12 \) gives \( 6:4:3 \).

reasoning: 20b + 16g = 18(b+g) gives 2b = 2g, so b = g and boys are 50% of the group.
solution: With \( b \) boys and \( g \) girls, \( 20b+16g=18(b+g) \), which simplifies to \( 2b=2g \), so \( b=g \). Boys therefore make up half the group, that is \( 50\% \).

reasoning: 2(l+b)h = 120 with h = 4 gives l+b = 15; l = 2b gives b = 5 and l = 10. Floor area = 50 square metres.
solution: The four walls have area \( 2(l+b)h=120 \), and with \( h=4 \) this gives \( l+b=15 \). Since the length is twice the breadth, \( 3b=15 \), so \( b=5 \) and \( l=10 \). The floor measures \( 10\times 5=50 \) square metres.

reasoning: In a circle of radius R, an inscribed square has diagonal 2R so x = R*sqrt2; an inscribed equilateral triangle has circumradius y/sqrt3 = R so y = R*sqrt3. Hence x/y = sqrt2/sqrt3 = sqrt(2/3).

solution: The sum of the cubes of the first \( n \) natural numbers is \( \left(\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)^{2} \), which for \( n=10 \) is \( 55^{2}=3025 \). The sum of the squares is \( \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}=385 \). The difference is \( 3025-385=2640 \).

solution: Because the same distance is covered at each speed, the average speed is the harmonic mean \( \dfrac{2\times 50\times 30}{50+30}=37.5 \) km/hour. The direct check agrees: the round trip of \( 300 \) km takes \( \dfrac{150}{50}+\dfrac{150}{30}=8 \) hours, and \( \dfrac{300}{8}=37.5 \) km/hour. The plain average of the two speeds would be \( 40 \), which is not the correct measure here.

solution: Work upwards from the bottom: \( 2+\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{7}{3} \), so \( \dfrac{1}{7/3}=\dfrac{3}{7} \) and \( 1+\dfrac{3}{7}=\dfrac{10}{7} \). The whole continued fraction is therefore \( \dfrac{7}{10} \), and the equation reads \( x+\dfrac{7}{10}=2 \). Hence \( x=\dfrac{13}{10} \).
